title: ParaLin++: Accelerating Parallel Diffusion Integrator via Intrinsic Partially Linear Structure

paper.title: ParaLin++: Accelerating Parallel Diffusion Integrator via Intrinsic Partially Linear Structure
paper.abstract: Abstract Training-free few-step samplers are often described as nearly quality-lossless under conventional FID/CLIP-style evaluation. It remains unclear whether that conclusion transfers to more realistic and complex generation-quality benchmarks. We first systematize the quality metrics used to evaluate training-free sampling acceleration for diffusion and flow-matching models. We find that representative training-free step-shortening methods often remain nearly lossless under FID/CLIP-class metrics, yet can suffer substantial quality degradation when evaluated with semantic-composition, dense-instruction, and long-text-rendering benchmarks such as GenEval, DPG-Bench, and LongTextBench. Parallel sampling is a notable exception: by retaining the full-step discretization and removing only the solver’s temporal dependency, it can preserve near-lossless quality while accelerating sampling. Building on this observation, we propose ParaLin++ , a step-parity parallel sampler that preserves the full-step discretization while accelerating the solver iterations. Experiments across Stable Diffusion-v2, LSUN Church, FLUX.1-dev, and Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0 show that ParaLin++ preserves the full-step Euler quality profile at 2.6 × 2.6\times – 4.8 × 4.8\times , 1.68 × 1.68\times on FLUX, and 1.21 × 1.21\times on Ming. sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs) [ 22 , 60 ] are now widely used in image and video generation, including large flow-matching models such as FLUX [ 4 ] and Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0 [ 1 ] , with applications from high-fidelity synthesis [ 53 , 5 ] to molecular generation [ 68 , 50 ] and a broad range of generative tasks [ 69 , 39 , 43 , 9 , 44 , 70 , 37 ] . In practical use, sampling cost is a dominant inference bottleneck: each high-resolution sample requires a long sequence of neural function evaluations (NFEs), and the latency of this sequential trajectory constrains serving throughput, inference cost, and on-device feasibility. The reference discretization of a DPM is a fixed N N -step ODE/SDE integrator, typically Euler with N = 30 N{=}30 steps for flow-matching models. Accelerating this pipeline has followed two structurally different routes, alongside a broader landscape of training-free speedups [ 16 , 75 , 17 , 13 , 39 , 47 ] . The first route shortens the discretization : high-order or few-step training-free solvers such as DDIM [ 57 ] , DPMSolver [ 42 , 41 ] , and UniPC [ 73 ] , together with distillation/consistency approaches [ 54 , 58 , 35 , 38 ] , cut the step count at the cost of changing the discretized trajectory. The second route removes solver latency instead : parallel sampling refines many time points concurrently, beginning with Picard iteration in ParaDiGMS [ 56 ] and progressing through triangular [ 62 ] and banded [ 45 ] nonlinear solvers, recently made NFE-efficient by the partial-linear formulation of ParaLin [ 46 ] . These two routes buy speed from different places: the first spends fewer integration steps , the second spends parallel compute to erase the solver’s temporal dependency . The decisive axis of a training-free accelerator is the metric that certifies it “quality-lossless,” not the speed lever it uses. Much of the literature uses distributional and coarse text-alignment proxies—FID measures closeness of the generated distribution to a reference, while CLIP measures coarse prompt–image embedding similarity. Post-trained text-to-image models, however, are often judged on a broader generation-quality profile: semantic composition (GenEval [ 15 ] ), dense instruction following (DPG-Bench [ 23 ] ), and long in-image text rendering (LongTextBench [ 14 ] ). A step-shortening strategy that looks lossless under FID can still alter the prompt-conditioned trajectory and produce a failed generation, because it changes the discrete trajectory on which prompt and text fidelity depend even when the marginal image distribution is preserved. We therefore focus on step-parity parallelization: keep the complete fixed-step system, but solve its coupled integration equations in parallel so that latency is removed without changing the discretization on which prompt-level and in-image text fidelity depend. Our contributions. We make the following contributions. 1 . A metric systemization and motivating finding. We systematize the quality metrics used to evaluate training-free sampling acceleration for diffusion and flow-matching models. Table I enumerates the evaluation protocols of a broad set of samplers—DDPM, DDIM, DPM-Solver, DPMSolver++, DPM-Solver-v3, UniPC, distillation and consistency methods, ParaDiGMS, ParaSolver, ParaLin, and ours—and shows that acceleration claims are usually certified by FID/CLIP-class metrics. These metrics measure statistical alignment or coarse prompt–image similarity; they do not directly measure semantic composition, dense instruction following, or in-image text rendering. Throughout, “complex generation quality” refers specifically to these three measurable axes rather than to an exhaustive definition of generation quality. Prior FID-oriented evaluations of DDIM, DPMSolver, DPMSolver++, and UniPC often report that few-step configurations remain close to the reference distribution [ 57 , 42 , 41 , 73 ] . Together with Table VI , this literature motivates a stricter audit: a 16-step DPMSolver++ configuration loses 21 % 21\% – 24 % 24\% GenEval, 6.5 6.5 – 8.2 8.2 DPG-Bench points, and 67 % 67\% – 70 % 70\% LongTextBench. Thus, the usual quality-lossless claim does not automatically transfer from FID/CLIP-style evidence to complex generation-quality benchmarks. A stronger step-parity parallel solver, ParaLin++. We build the strongest available realization of the step-parity route to test how far this route reaches. Starting from ParaLin’s ϱ \varrho -nonlinear partial-linear system, we add an adaptive nonlinearization iteration, a successive-over-relaxation (SOR) update for both nonlinear and linear blocks, a sliding window, and an adaptive stopping rule based on relative historical errors and an exponential moving average. We prove that the SOR update is stable for 0 < ω < 2 / ( 1 + L ) 0<\omega<2/(1+L) (contraction factor L < 1 L<1 ) and that the system admits the sequential trajectory as its unique convergent root. 3 . A quality–speed audit on realistic generation benchmarks. We evaluate Stable Diffusion-v2, LSUN Church, FLUX.1-dev, Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0, five CFG values, three complex-generation benchmarks, visual comparisons, and ablations. Our key lessons are: 1. FID/CLIP agreement does not imply generation-quality preservation. On FLUX, a 1.8 × 1.8\times few-step claim that is valid under FID coincides with a 21 % 21\% – 24 % 24\% GenEval drop, a 6.5 6.5 – 8.2 8.2 DPG-Bench point drop, and a 67 % 67\% – 70 % 70\% LongTextBench drop—an operational failure the standard evaluation hides. 2. Step-parity keeps the reference profile. Keeping all 30 steps and parallel-solving gives 1.68 × 1.68\times on FLUX and 1.21 × 1.21\times on Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0 with an Euler-level generation-quality profile ( 0.64 0.64 vs. 0.66 0.66 GenEval, 84.24 84.24 vs. 83.97 83.97 DPG, 0.26 0.26 vs. 0.27 0.27 LTB), and 2.6 × 2.6\times – 4.8 × 4.8\times on Stable Diffusion-v2/LSUN Church. 3. Guidance sharpens the quality gap. Across CFG 0 0 – 14 14 , the completed DPG-Bench matrix shows ParaLin++ tracking Euler closely ( 82.18 82.18 – 84.24 84.24 vs. 82.25 82.25 – 83.97 83.97 ) while 20-step UniPC/DPMSolver++ drop to 68.85 68.85 – 79.67 79.67 . 4. Report iterations and generation-quality metrics, not only FID. A speedup claim should separate discrete steps from solver iterations/NFE and be measured against the same-CFG 30-step Euler reference on a generation-quality benchmark; FID-only evidence is not sufficient to establish quality preservation. Implications of our study. Representative training-free step-shortening methods can appear nearly lossless under FID/CLIP yet show substantial degradation on more realistic and complex quality benchmarks. This argues for reporting generation-quality results alongside FID and for treating step-parity parallel sampling as an exception that can preserve near-lossless quality while accelerating sampling. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II provides the necessary background and reviews existing training-free accelerators. Section III systematizes the quality metrics used to evaluate training-free acceleration and shows that FID-matched step shortening can incur large quality degradation on complex-generation benchmarks. Section IV first reviews ParaLin’s partial-linear reformulation and then designs the stronger parallel solver ParaLin++ (Section IV-B ). Section V reports the quality–speed audit on complex-generation benchmarks and ablations. Section VI concludes this paper. Complete derivations and proofs of the propositions in Section IV are provided in Appendices A–D of the separate supplementary material.

sections.heading: II-A Existing Training-Free Accelerators
sections.text: Step-parity temporal parallelization. Parallel sampling removes the temporal dependency of a fixed-step diffusion integrator by refining multiple time states concurrently. ParaDiGMS [ 56 ] introduced this direction through Picard–Lindelöf fixed-point iteration; Self-Refining Diffusion Samplers [ 55 ] use Parareal iterations; ParaTAA [ 62 ] formulates a triangular nonlinear system; and ParaSolver [ 45 ] improves efficiency through banded and hierarchical parallelization. CHORDS [ 19 ] further treats multi-core sampling as a hierarchy of increasingly accurate solvers, whereas ParaAnya [ 71 ] uses a plug-and-play output cache to avoid repeated evaluations at overlapping timesteps. These methods reinforce the same trade-off as ParaDiGMS: additional parallel compute replaces sequential time, rather than coarsening the integration grid. ParaLin [ 46 ] reduces the NFE overhead of fully nonlinear iterations by exploiting partial linearity; ParaLin++ strengthens this solver with adaptive nonlinearization, over-relaxation, and adaptive stopping. A closely related but distinct solver is EPD [ 78 ] , which evaluates multiple gradient directions concurrently inside each ODE step and learns a small set of solver parameters through distillation. Unlike step-parity methods, it changes the local integration rule and requires a lightweight training stage. Recent theory also cautions against an unconstrained parallelization story: parallel-round lower bounds [ 31 ] show that some distributions necessarily retain polynomial sequential dependence. ParaLin++ is therefore formulated as a practical fixed-step parallel integrator, not as a claim that all diffusion sampling can be made depth-free. Speculative and asynchronous parallelism. A second parallel family drafts approximate future states and verifies or refines them in parallel. Diffusion speculative sampling [ 11 ] preserves the target distribution by accepting or correcting draft proposals; FREE [ 67 ] extends this idea to feature-level autoregression in DiTs; SpecDiff [ 51 ] combines self-speculation with feature caching; and DRiffusion [ 3 ] uses a draft-and-refine process. AsyncDiff [ 8 ] instead breaks component dependencies through asynchronous denoising. These methods exploit drafts, verifiers, or stale hidden states, and thus change the execution graph; ParaLin++ solves the coupled fixed-step integration system directly and does not introduce an auxiliary drafter. Step-shortening solvers and schedules. Classical high-order ODE samplers shorten the timestep grid [ 57 , 42 , 41 , 73 ] . Recent training-free variants improve this route through adaptive flow paths [ 27 ] , multirate integration for the guidance branch [ 32 ] , stiffness-aware integration [ 61 ] , and hierarchical timestep-schedule optimization [ 77 ] . These methods are relevant baselines for the quality audit, but they still alter the discretization on which prompt-conditioned trajectories depend. Per-step compute reduction and model parallelism. Orthogonal accelerators reduce the cost of each denoising evaluation. They include feature and block caching [ 49 , 48 , 40 ] , DiT attention or token sparsification [ 74 , 26 ] , temporal feature forecasting [ 36 , 18 ] , path-planned cache scheduling [ 10 ] , and distributed or asynchronous execution [ 33 , 66 , 8 ] . Guidance acceleration [ 65 ] , trajectory stitching [ 52 ] , nested diffusion [ 12 ] , and minimum-step prediction [ 72 ] are likewise complementary. These systems change the executed network path or decide when a cheaper computation is acceptable; ParaLin++ changes neither the timestep grid nor the full-step denoiser evaluation. Quality-focused evaluation. The claim that FID/CLIP evidence is insufficient is consistent with the evaluation literature: TIFA uses visual question answering to test fine-grained prompt faithfulness [ 24 ] ; VQAScore and GenAI-Bench target compositional prompts [ 34 ] ; and T2I-CompBench++ evaluates attributes, relations, and numeracy [ 25 ] . GenEval 2 additionally warns that static benchmarks can drift as generation models improve [ 28 ] . Our audit therefore interprets GenEval, DPG-Bench, and LongTextBench as a fixed, reproducible quality profile rather than as an absolute or exhaustive definition of generation quality.

sections.heading: III Systemization of Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration
sections.text: We systematize training-free diffusion acceleration through the quality metrics on which its “quality-lossless” claims rest, rather than through the speed lever it uses, because FID/CLIP-style evidence does not by itself establish preservation on complex prompts. We first enumerate the evaluation protocols of the academic acceleration literature (Table I ) and identify what these methods actually measure; we then test representative few-step quality claims under a generation-quality audit and find substantial degradation (Section V , summarized in Table VI ).

sections.heading: III-A Quality Metrics in the Training-Free Acceleration Literature
sections.text: Table I surveys the quality metrics used to evaluate a broad set of training-free samplers and their close relatives, from DDPM and DDIM through high-order solvers (DPM-Solver, DPMSolver++, DPM-Solver-v3, UniPC) and distillation/consistency methods, to parallel samplers (ParaDiGMS, ParaTAA, ParaSolver, ParaLin) and our ParaLin++. Two patterns are immediate. First , nearly every method is evaluated with distributional and text-alignment metrics only: FID (and its variants sFID, clean-FID) measures closeness of the generated distribution to a reference distribution, while CLIP score/CLIP-FID measures coarse prompt–image embedding similarity, and a handful additionally report Inception-based diversity (IS, Precision–Recall). These quantify statistical alignment —whether the marginal image distribution or the prompt–image embedding stays close to a reference—not whether a specific generated sample succeeds at semantic composition, dense instruction following, or long-text rendering. Second , few methods explicitly audit these generation-quality dimensions. Recent large-scale models such as FLUX [ 4 ] and Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0 [ 1 ] , in contrast, report GenEval-, DPG-Bench-, and LongTextBench-style numbers, whereas FID/CLIP are scarce or absent in their evaluation reports. A sampler certified only by FID/CLIP-style metrics can therefore appear lossless while remaining fragile on complex prompts.

sections.heading: III-B A Realistic Quality Audit of Training-Free Accelerators
sections.text: The metrics gap is not cosmetic. We further test the same training-free accelerators under the generation-quality profile—GenEval, DPG-Bench, and LongTextBench—on the high-capacity FLUX.1-dev [ 4 ] , against the same-CFG 30-step Euler reference; the result is summarized in Table VI and elaborated in Section V . Methods advertised as nearly quality-lossless under FID show substantial degradation on the generation-quality metrics. Prior FID-oriented evaluations support the general expectation that reduced-step configurations can remain close to the reference distribution [ 57 , 42 , 41 , 73 ] ; in our audit, however, 16-step UniPC and DPMSolver++ cause GenEval to fall from 0.66 0.66 to 0.50 0.50 – 0.52 0.52 , DPG-Bench from 83.97 83.97 to 75.75 75.75 – 77.46 77.46 , and LongTextBench from 0.27 0.27 to 0.08 0.08 – 0.09 0.09 . An image distribution can stay FID-plausible while the model omits requested objects, breaks spatial relations, or renders unreadable text. Hence, representative training-free few-step solvers can appear nearly lossless under FID/CLIP yet lose substantially under realistic, complex quality metrics. Parallel sampling is an important exception: by preserving the full-step trajectory, it can retain near-lossless quality while removing solver latency. This failure is structural rather than incidental. Step-shortening solvers (DDIM, DPMSolver++, UniPC) buy fewer discrete steps by altering the prompt-conditioned trajectory, and the altered trajectory is what breaks dense-prompt and text fidelity; FID merely fails to reflect this break because it overlooks sample-level semantics. Parallel sampling instead keeps all N N discrete steps and removes only the solver’s temporal dependency, preserving the prompt-conditioned trajectory and the quality that depends on it. We call this the step-parity route, and ParaLin++ (Section IV-B ) is designed as its strongest realization. The rest of the paper extends the generation-quality audit (Section V ) and strengthens the step-parity solver (Sections IV – IV-B ).

sections.heading: IV-B Designing ParaLin++: A Stronger Step-Parity Solver
sections.text: ParaLin++ accelerates the ParaLin solver from two complementary perspectives. First, it retains ParaLin’s adaptive nonlinearization and immediate update strategy, which exploit the latest refined states within an iteration. Second, it introduces SOR and a relative adaptive stopping rule to reduce the remaining iterations. The sliding-window and initialization strategies are then integrated into the complete algorithm.

sections.heading: IV-B 1 Adaptive Nonlinearization Iteration
sections.text: We investigate the update rule in Eq. ( 5 ) to solve the prescribed ϱ \varrho -nonlinear system. Specializing Eq. ( 5 ) to our system yields the following iterative scheme: 𝐗 ^ t 0 : t N ( k + 1 ) = 𝐗 ^ t 0 : t N ( k ) − 𝒢 ( k ) ℛ t 0 : t N ( k ) , \hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{0}:t_{N}}^{(k+1)}=\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{0}:t_{N}}^{(k)}-\mathcal{G}^{(k)}\mathcal{R}_{t_{0}:t_{N}}^{(k)}, (14) where the residual term ℛ t n + 1 ( k ) \mathcal{R}_{t_{n+1}}^{(k)} with ℛ t 0 ( k ) = 𝐗 ^ t 0 ( k ) − 𝐗 t 0 = 0 \mathcal{R}_{t_{0}}^{(k)}=\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{0}}^{(k)}-\mathbf{X}_{t_{0}}=0 is defined as: ℛ t n + 1 ( k ) = { 𝐗 ^ t n + 1 ( k ) − ℋ n ​ ( 𝐗 ^ t n ( k ) , 𝒫 n ( k ) ) , n ∈ [ 0 , ϱ − 1 ] , 𝐗 ^ t n + 1 ( k ) − ℋ n ​ ( 𝐗 ^ t n ( k ) , 𝒫 ϱ − 1 ( k ) ) , n ∈ [ ϱ , N − 1 ] . \displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{t_{n+1}}^{(k)}=\begin{cases}\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{n+1}}^{(k)}-\mathcal{H}_{n}\bigl(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{n}}^{(k)},\mathcal{P}_{n}^{(k)}\bigr),&n\in[0,\varrho-1],\\ \hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{n+1}}^{(k)}-\mathcal{H}_{n}\bigl(\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{n}}^{(k)},\mathcal{P}_{\varrho-1}^{(k)}\bigr),&n\in[\varrho,N-1].\end{cases} (15) Observe that this update rule applies a Jacobi-type iteration, where all components 𝐗 t 1 : t N ( k + 1 ) \mathbf{X}_{t_{1}:t_{N}}^{(k+1)} are updated exclusively from the old components 𝐗 t 1 : t N ( k ) \mathbf{X}_{t_{1}:t_{N}}^{(k)} , resulting in delayed information propagation across time steps. Inspired by the classical Gauss-Seidel iteration, we propose a more efficient immediate update strategy wherein newly updated components are incorporated immediately into subsequent components’ updating within the same iteration. Specifically, we first update the nonlinear-region components 𝐗 t n ( k ) \mathbf{X}_{t_{n}}^{(k)} for n ∈ { 1 , ⋯ , ϱ } n\in\{1,\cdots,\varrho\} . sections.heading: IV-B 2 Convergence Acceleration via Successive Over-Relaxation
sections.text: While the immediate update strategy enhances information flow within each iteration, the solver may still require a considerable number of iterations ( K K ) to converge, particularly for high-dimensional problems. To further reduce the iteration count, we incorporate the Successive Over-Relaxation (SOR) method, a well-established technique for accelerating the convergence of iterative solvers. The core idea is to introduce a relaxation factor ω \omega to extrapolate the update step, pushing the solution more aggressively towards the root. The standard Gauss-Seidel-like update can be viewed as a two-step process. First, an intermediate state 𝐙 ^ ( k + 1 ) \hat{\mathbf{Z}}^{(k+1)} is computed based on the residual: 𝐙 ^ ( k + 1 ) = 𝐗 ^ ( k ) − 𝒢 ( k ) ​ ℛ ( k ) . \hat{\mathbf{Z}}^{(k+1)}=\hat{\mathbf{X}}^{(k)}-\mathcal{G}^{(k)}\mathcal{R}^{(k)}. (20) The SOR update then modifies this step by taking a weighted average of the current state 𝐗 ^ ( k ) \hat{\mathbf{X}}^{(k)} and the intermediate state 𝐙 ^ ( k + 1 ) \hat{\mathbf{Z}}^{(k+1)} : 𝐗 ^ ( k + 1 ) = ( 1 − ω ) ​ 𝐗 ^ ( k ) + ω ​ 𝐙 ^ ( k + 1 ) , \hat{\mathbf{X}}^{(k+1)}=(1-\omega)\hat{\mathbf{X}}^{(k)}+\omega\hat{\mathbf{Z}}^{(k+1)}, (21) where ω \omega is the relaxation factor. Setting ω = 1 \omega=1 recovers the original update rule, while ω > 1 \omega>1 (over-relaxation) typically accelerates convergence for the systems encountered in our problem. We now integrate this SOR mechanism into our solver for both the nonlinear and linear components. Update for Nonlinear Components. For the first ϱ \varrho components within the current window, which are processed in parallel, we first compute their intermediate states based on the nonlinear residuals defined in Eq. ( 19 ): 𝐙 ^ t n + 1 : t n + ϱ ( k + 1 ) = 𝐗 ^ t n + 1 : t n + ϱ ( k ) − 𝒢 ( k ) ℛ t n + 1 : t n + ϱ ( k ) . \hat{\mathbf{Z}}_{t_{n+1}:t_{n+\varrho}}^{(k+1)}=\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{n+1}:t_{n+\varrho}}^{(k)}-\mathcal{G}^{(k)}\mathcal{R}_{t_{n+1}:t_{n+\varrho}}^{(k)}. (22) Subsequently, we apply the SOR update to obtain the refined states for the nonlinear block: 𝐗 ^ t n + 1 : t n + ϱ ( k + 1 ) = ( 1 − ω ) 𝐗 ^ t n + 1 : t n + ϱ ( k ) + ω 𝐙 ^ t n + 1 : t n + ϱ ( k + 1 ) . \hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{n+1}:t_{n+\varrho}}^{(k+1)}=(1-\omega)\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{n+1}:t_{n+\varrho}}^{(k)}+\omega\hat{\mathbf{Z}}_{t_{n+1}:t_{n+\varrho}}^{(k+1)}. (23) Update for Linear Components. For the remaining components ( i ∈ [ n + ϱ , N − 1 ] i\in[n+\varrho,N-1] ), we combine the SOR method with the immediate update strategy. These components are updated sequentially, allowing the most recent information to propagate immediately. For each linear component, we compute the intermediate state: 𝐙 ^ t i + 1 ( k + 1 ) = 𝐗 ^ t i + 1 ( k ) − 𝒢 ( k ) ​ ℛ t i + 1 ( k ) , \hat{\mathbf{Z}}_{t_{i+1}}^{(k+1)}=\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{i+1}}^{(k)}-\mathcal{G}^{(k)}\mathcal{R}_{t_{i+1}}^{(k)}, (24) where the residual ℛ t i + 1 ( k ) \mathcal{R}_{t_{i+1}}^{(k)} is computed using the already updated value 𝐗 ^ t i ( k + 1 ) \hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{i}}^{(k+1)} , as specified in Eq. ( 19 ). The final updated state is then obtained via the SOR formulation: 𝐗 ^ t i + 1 ( k + 1 ) = ( 1 − ω ) ​ 𝐗 ^ t i + 1 ( k ) + ω ​ 𝐙 ^ t i + 1 ( k + 1 ) . \hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{i+1}}^{(k+1)}=(1-\omega)\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{i+1}}^{(k)}+\omega\hat{\mathbf{Z}}_{t_{i+1}}^{(k+1)}. (25) By integrating SOR, our proposed solver, ParaLin++, significantly reduces the number of iterations K K required to reach the desired tolerance, thereby providing a substantial improvement in overall sampling efficiency without compromising the quality of the generated samples. sections.heading: IV-B 4 Adaptive Stopping Criterion
sections.text: Prior works [ 56 , 62 , 45 ] typically employ a single tolerance, denoted as δ \delta , to control the state difference across all timesteps. However, we find that this coarse-grained method cannot accurately identify states that have already converged, leading to superfluous iteration steps to update them. To address this inefficiency, we introduce a more fine-grained, adaptive stopping criterion. Our approach is based on the principle of relative reduction to a historical average. Instead of comparing the current update error to a fixed threshold, we evaluate it against a fraction of the average historical error. This allows the criterion to dynamically adjust to the convergence progress. Fig. 1: Illustration of ParaLin++. During iteration k k , ParaLin++ performs simultaneous denoising updates across multiple steps. From left to right: existing full nonlinear parallel methods, our partial linear method, and our method for faster convergence. Specifically, following [ 56 , 62 , 45 ] , let the error of state 𝐗 ^ t i \hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{i}} at iteration k ∈ [ 0 , K ] k\in[0,K] be defined as: ℰ t i ( k ) = 1 D ​ σ t i 2 ​ ‖ 𝐗 ^ t i ( k + 1 ) − 𝐗 ^ t i ( k ) ‖ F 2 , \mathcal{E}^{(k)}_{t_{i}}=\frac{1}{D\sigma^{2}_{t_{i}}}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{i}}^{(k+1)}-\hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{i}}^{(k)}\right\|_{F}^{2}, where D D is the dimensionality of the state 𝐗 ^ t i \hat{\mathbf{X}}_{t_{i}} and ∥ ⋅ ∥ F \|\cdot\|_{F} denotes the Frobenius norm. We maintain a running average of all historical errors, ℰ ¯ t i \bar{\mathcal{E}}_{t_{i}} , up to the current iteration k k : ℰ ¯ t i = 1 k + 1 ​ ∑ j = 0 k ℰ t i ( j ) . \bar{\mathcal{E}}_{t_{i}}=\frac{1}{k+1}\sum_{j=0}^{k}\mathcal{E}^{(j)}_{t_{i}}. The stopping condition is then met when the current error, ℰ t i ( k ) \mathcal{E}^{(k)}_{t_{i}} , is significantly smaller than this historical error average, scaled by a tolerance δ \delta : ℰ t i ( k ) ≤ δ ⋅ ℰ ¯ t i . \mathcal{E}^{(k)}_{t_{i}}\leq\delta\cdot\bar{\mathcal{E}}_{t_{i}}. Furthermore, the tolerance δ \delta is not a fixed hyperparameter but is itself updated adaptively to refine the stopping condition. We introduce an update mechanism with an EDM (Exponential Decay Mean) decay rate, β \beta , which allows the tolerance to respond to the recent convergence behavior. The tolerance for the next step, δ \delta , is updated as follows: δ = β ​ δ + ( 1 − β ) ⋅ ℳ ⁡ ( { ℰ t i ( k ) ∣ i ∈ [ n , n + p − 1 ] } ) , \delta=\beta\delta+(1-\beta)\cdot\mathcal{M}\Big(\big\{\mathcal{E}^{(k)}_{t_{i}}\mid i\in[n,n+p-1]\big\}\Big), where ℳ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{M}(\cdot) computes the median value which provides a robust estimate of recent error. This dual-adaptive strategy, comparing to the historical average and dynamically updating the tolerance threshold, enables a more efficient convergence. We empirically find it terminates iterations more precisely when a state has stabilized, thereby reducing the number of steps required while preserving sample quality.

sections.heading: V-A Experiment Settings
sections.text: Evaluation Metrics and Datasets. We report function evaluations (NFEs), iterations, wall-clock time, FID [ 21 ] , and CLIP score [ 20 ] . For Stable Diffusion-v2 and LSUN Church, FID and CLIP are computed on 5000 random samples, using ImageNet-1k with classifier guidance w = 7.5 w=7.5 and the LSUN model, respectively. For FLUX, FID is computed on 5000 FluxPrompting [ 63 ] samples for the 12B model [ 4 ] . The CIFAR-10 less-step study uses 50,000 samples, as reported in Table V . For generation-quality-focused evaluation, we additionally report GenEval [ 15 ] , DPG-Bench [ 23 ] , and LongTextBench [ 14 ] , which assess semantic composition, dense instruction following, and long in-image text rendering, respectively. Models. The evaluation covers latent-space Stable Diffusion-v2, CIFAR-10, the 12B FLUX flow-matching model, the pixel-space LSUN Church model, and VP/VE/EDM processes. The generation-quality study centers on FLUX and uses the Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0 generator [ 1 ] as a second large-scale reference model. Algorithms. ParaLin++ is applied to DDIM [ 57 ] and DPMSolver [ 42 ] . It is compared with ParaLin [ 46 ] , ParaDiGMS [ 56 ] , ParaSolver [ 45 ] , and relevant few-step solvers. All compared baseline samplers are invoked through the official implementations integrated in the Diffusers library [ 64 ] ; we do not use custom re-implementations of the baseline solvers. Hyperparameters. Following [ 45 , 62 ] , we use the best tolerances reported for ParaDiGMS and ParaSolver. For ParaLin++, we set ϱ = 8 \varrho=8 unless otherwise specified, use eight NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs for multi-GPU settings, and search δ \delta , β \beta , and ω \omega independently for each sampler. Additional details are given in the supplementary material. FLUX generation-quality benchmark protocol. The FLUX.1-dev study uses 1024 × 1024 1024{\times}1024 generation with guidance scale 3.5 3.5 on eight GPUs. The Euler sampler with 30 discrete diffusion steps is the reference. UniPC and DPM-Solver++ are evaluated with their standard sequential few-step samplers at 16 , 20 , 24 , 26 16,20,24,26 , and 30 30 discrete diffusion steps. ParaLin++ keeps 30 discrete diffusion steps and uses the proposed parallel solver with tolerance δ = 0.01 \delta=0.01 , nonlinear-transition parameter ϱ = 1 \varrho=1 , parallel window size p = 100 p=100 , and a solver-step cap of 1000 1000 . LongTextBench is the average of the English and Chinese text scores. Speedup is measured from the sampler/model forward-path time of the GenEval generation pass and excludes model loading and scoring; these timing measurements are used consistently across the detailed FLUX table. Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0 generation-quality benchmark protocol. The Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0 study uses the Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0 generator at 1024 × 1024 1024{\times}1024 with guidance scale 5.0 5.0 on eight GPUs. Euler, UniPC, and DPM-Solver++ are evaluated with their standard sequential samplers at the listed step settings. ParaLin++ keeps 30 discrete diffusion steps and uses the proposed parallel solver with tolerance δ = 0.01 \delta=0.01 , nonlinear-transition parameter ϱ = 1 \varrho=1 , parallel window size p = 100 p=100 , and a solver-step cap of 1000 1000 . LongTextBench uses 320 prompts with 4 images each, seed 42, hybrid OCR, a bounding-box score threshold of 0.85 0.85 , and reports the average of the English and Chinese scores. DPG-Bench uses 1065 images with the mPLUG visual-question-answering model. GenEval uses 553 prompts with 4 images each, bf16 generation, and 8 evaluation workers. The table reports the complete 16 16 -, 20 20 -, 24 24 -, 26 26 -, and 30 30 -step quality matrix. All speedup values use the CFG-5 GenEval generation pass against the 30 30 -step Euler reference, excluding model loading and scoring.

However, our experiments in Table IX demonstrate the real-world viability of our approach on a single GPU. Unlike competing parallel methods like ParaDiGMS, which often fail to provide any speedup or even decelerate the process in this setting, our ParaLin++ achieves consistent and significant wall-clock acceleration across all baseline samplers. This is accomplished while maintaining virtually identical generation quality (FID and CLIP scores). This validates ParaLin++ as a practical and potent accelerator for everyday users, effectively overcoming the typical computational barriers of parallel sampling even in resource-constrained, single-GPU environments. Generalization on VP, VE, and EDM Process. We investigated the impact of the VP, VE, and EDM diffusion processes by converting the sequential sampler in Alg. 1 of work [ 29 ] into our parallel version. Adopting the Tab. 1 configurations specified in work [ 29 ] , we then analyzed the effect of the nonlinear degree ϱ \varrho on FID performance across these three processes using the provided ImageNet dataset. As shown in Tab. XI , our parallel sampling method demonstrates its applicability and effectiveness across all three diffusion processes. For each process, our parallel approach consistently reduces the number of sampling iterations while achieving comparable or improved FID scores compared to the sequential baseline. This highlights the robustness and efficiency of our method, making it a viable accelerator for various diffusion model formulations. We notice that our method yields a better FID score for every schedule and a substantially larger gain in the VP process. This improvement likely stems from the inherently stiff nature of the VP-ODE, combined with the step-parallel updates of our parallel solver. The step-parallel updates sever the temporal dependence chain across steps, thus effectively curtail the accumulation of truncation error across steps [ 29 ] . As a result, our solver acts as an implicit numerical stabilizer for the stiff VP-ODE, which typically exhibits significant truncation error that degrades the performance of conventional VP samplers. sections.heading: VI Conclusion
sections.text: We systematized training-free diffusion acceleration by the metrics that certify its quality-preservation claims, exposing heavy reliance on FID/CLIP-style evidence. Our generation-quality audit shows that representative few-step solvers can remain FID-close yet lose substantial semantic-composition, instruction-following, and long-text-rendering quality. To accelerate without shortening the trajectory, ParaLin++ strengthens ParaLin’s partial-linear solver with adaptive nonlinearization, successive over-relaxation, sliding windows, and adaptive stopping, supported by stability and uniqueness guarantees. It preserves the full-step quality profile while reaching 1.68 × 1.68\times on FLUX.1-dev, 1.21 × 1.21\times on Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0, and 2.6 × 2.6\times – 4.8 × 4.8\times on Stable Diffusion-v2/LSUN Church. Acceleration claims should therefore report generation-quality metrics alongside FID/CLIP and separate discrete steps from solver iterations.

Abstract Training-free few-step samplers are often described as nearly quality-lossless under conventional FID/CLIP-style evaluation. It remains unclear whether that conclusion transfers to more realistic and complex generation-quality benchmarks. We first systematize the quality metrics used to evaluate training-free sampling acceleration for diffusion and flow-matching models. We find that representative training-free step-shortening methods often remain nearly lossless under FID/CLIP-class metrics, yet can suffer substantial quality degradation when evaluated with semantic-composition, dense-instruction, and long-text-rendering benchmarks such as GenEval, DPG-Bench, and LongTextBench. Parallel sampling is a notable exception: by retaining the full-step discretization and removing only the solver’s temporal dependency, it can preserve near-lossless quality while accelerating sampling. Building on this observation, we propose ParaLin++ , a step-parity parallel sampler that preserves the full-step discretization while accelerating the solver iterations. Experiments across Stable Diffusion-v2, LSUN Church, FLUX.1-dev, and Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0 show that ParaLin++ preserves the full-step Euler quality profile at 2.6 × 2.6\times – 4.8 × 4.8\times , 1.68 × 1.68\times on FLUX, and 1.21 × 1.21\times on Ming. Index Terms: Diffusion Probabilistic Models, Parallel Sampling, Generative Models, Model Acceleration, Ordinary Differential Equations, System of Linear Equations. I Introduction Diffusion probabilistic models (DPMs) [ 22 , 60 ] are now widely used in image and video generation, including large flow-matching models such as FLUX [ 4 ] and Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0 [ 1 ] , with applications from high-fidelity synthesis [ 53 , 5 ] to molecular generation [ 68 , 50 ] and a broad range of generative tasks [ 69 , 39 , 43 , 9 , 44 , 70 , 37 ] . In practical use, sampling cost is a dominant inference bottleneck: each high-resolution sample requires a long sequence of neural function evaluations (NFEs), and the latency of this sequential trajectory constrains serving throughput, inference cost, and on-device feasibility. The reference discretization of a DPM is a fixed N N -step ODE/SDE integrator, typically Euler with N = 30 N{=}30 steps for flow-matching models. Accelerating this pipeline has followed two structurally different routes, alongside a broader landscape of training-free speedups [ 16 , 75 , 17 , 13 , 39 , 47 ] . The first route shortens the discretization : high-order or few-step training-free solvers such as DDIM [ 57 ] , DPMSolver [ 42 , 41 ] , and UniPC [ 73 ] , together with distillation/consistency approaches [ 54 , 58 , 35 , 38 ] , cut the step count at the cost of changing the discretized trajectory. The second route removes solver latency instead : parallel sampling refines many time points concurrently, beginning with Picard iteration in ParaDiGMS [ 56 ] and progressing through triangular [ 62 ] and banded [ 45 ] nonlinear solvers, recently made NFE-efficient by the partial-linear formulation of ParaLin [ 46 ] . These two routes buy speed from different places: the first spends fewer integration steps , the second spends parallel compute to erase the solver’s temporal dependency . The decisive axis of a training-free accelerator is the metric that certifies it “quality-lossless,” not the speed lever it uses. Much of the literature uses distributional and coarse text-alignment proxies—FID measures closeness of the generated distribution to a reference, while CLIP measures coarse prompt–image embedding similarity. Post-trained text-to-image models, however, are often judged on a broader generation-quality profile: semantic composition (GenEval [ 15 ] ), dense instruction following (DPG-Bench [ 23 ] ), and long in-image text rendering (LongTextBench [ 14 ] ). A step-shortening strategy that looks lossless under FID can still alter the prompt-conditioned trajectory and produce a failed generation, because it changes the discrete trajectory on which prompt and text fidelity depend even when the marginal image distribution is preserved. We therefore focus on step-parity parallelization: keep the complete fixed-step system, but solve its coupled integration equations in parallel so that latency is removed without changing the discretization on which prompt-level and in-image text fidelity depend. Our contributions. We make the following contributions. 1 . A metric systemization and motivating finding. We systematize the quality metrics used to evaluate training-free sampling acceleration for diffusion and flow-matching models. Table I enumerates the evaluation protocols of a broad set of samplers—DDPM, DDIM, DPM-Solver, DPMSolver++, DPM-Solver-v3, UniPC, distillation and consistency methods, ParaDiGMS, ParaSolver, ParaLin, and ours—and shows that acceleration claims are usually certified by FID/CLIP-class metrics. These metrics measure statistical alignment or coarse prompt–image similarity; they do not directly measure semantic composition, dense instruction following, or in-image text rendering. Throughout, “complex generation quality” refers specifically to these three measurable axes rather than to an exhaustive definition of generation quality. Prior FID-oriented evaluations of DDIM, DPMSolver, DPMSolver++, and UniPC often report that few-step configurations remain close to the reference distribution [ 57 , 42 , 41 , 73 ] . Together with Table VI , this literature motivates a stricter audit: a 16-step DPMSolver++ configuration loses 21 % 21\% – 24 % 24\% GenEval, 6.5 6.5 – 8.2 8.2 DPG-Bench points, and 67 % 67\% – 70 % 70\% LongTextBench. Thus, the usual quality-lossless claim does not automatically transfer from FID/CLIP-style evidence to complex generation-quality benchmarks. A stronger step-parity parallel solver, ParaLin++. We build the strongest available realization of the step-parity route to test how far this route reaches. Starting from ParaLin’s ϱ \varrho -nonlinear partial-linear system, we add an adaptive nonlinearization iteration, a successive-over-relaxation (SOR) update for both nonlinear and linear blocks, a sliding window, and an adaptive stopping rule based on relative historical errors and an exponential moving average. We prove that the SOR update is stable for 0 < ω < 2 / ( 1 + L ) 0<\omega<2/(1+L) (contraction factor L < 1 L<1 ) and that the system admits the sequential trajectory as its unique convergent root. 3 . A quality–speed audit on realistic generation benchmarks. We evaluate Stable Diffusion-v2, LSUN Church, FLUX.1-dev, Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0, five CFG values, three complex-generation benchmarks, visual comparisons, and ablations. Our key lessons are: 1. FID/CLIP agreement does not imply generation-quality preservation. On FLUX, a 1.8 × 1.8\times few-step claim that is valid under FID coincides with a 21 % 21\% – 24 % 24\% GenEval drop, a 6.5 6.5 – 8.2 8.2 DPG-Bench point drop, and a 67 % 67\% – 70 % 70\% LongTextBench drop—an operational failure the standard evaluation hides. 2. Step-parity keeps the reference profile. Keeping all 30 steps and parallel-solving gives 1.68 × 1.68\times on FLUX and 1.21 × 1.21\times on Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0 with an Euler-level generation-quality profile ( 0.64 0.64 vs. 0.66 0.66 GenEval, 84.24 84.24 vs. 83.97 83.97 DPG, 0.26 0.26 vs. 0.27 0.27 LTB), and 2.6 × 2.6\times – 4.8 × 4.8\times on Stable Diffusion-v2/LSUN Church. 3. Guidance sharpens the quality gap. Across CFG 0 0 – 14 14 , the completed DPG-Bench matrix shows ParaLin++ tracking Euler closely ( 82.18 82.18 – 84.24 84.24 vs. 82.25 82.25 – 83.97 83.97 ) while 20-step UniPC/DPMSolver++ drop to 68.85 68.85 – 79.67 79.67 . 4. Report iterations and generation-quality metrics, not only FID. A speedup claim should separate discrete steps from solver iterations/NFE and be measured against the same-CFG 30-step Euler reference on a generation-quality benchmark; FID-only evidence is not sufficient to establish quality preservation. Implications of our study. Representative training-free step-shortening methods can appear nearly lossless under FID/CLIP yet show substantial degradation on more realistic and complex quality benchmarks. This argues for reporting generation-quality results alongside FID and for treating step-parity parallel sampling as an exception that can preserve near-lossless quality while accelerating sampling. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II provides the necessary background and reviews existing training-free accelerators. Section III systematizes the quality metrics used to evaluate training-free acceleration and shows that FID-matched step shortening can incur large quality degradation on complex-generation benchmarks. Section IV first reviews ParaLin’s partial-linear reformulation and then designs the stronger parallel solver ParaLin++ (Section IV-B ). Section V reports the quality–speed audit on complex-generation benchmarks and ablations. Section VI concludes this paper. II-A Existing Training-Free Accelerators Step-parity temporal parallelization. Parallel sampling removes the temporal dependency of a fixed-step diffusion integrator by refining multiple time states concurrently. ParaDiGMS [ 56 ] introduced this direction through Picard–Lindelöf fixed-point iteration; Self-Refining Diffusion Samplers [ 55 ] use Parareal iterations; ParaTAA [ 62 ] formulates a triangular nonlinear system; and ParaSolver [ 45 ] improves efficiency through banded and hierarchical parallelization. CHORDS [ 19 ] further treats multi-core sampling as a hierarchy of increasingly accurate solvers, whereas ParaAnya [ 71 ] uses a plug-and-play output cache to avoid repeated evaluations at overlapping timesteps. These methods reinforce the same trade-off as ParaDiGMS: additional parallel compute replaces sequential time, rather than coarsening the integration grid. ParaLin [ 46 ] reduces the NFE overhead of fully nonlinear iterations by exploiting partial linearity; ParaLin++ strengthens this solver with adaptive nonlinearization, over-relaxation, and adaptive stopping. A closely related but distinct solver is EPD [ 78 ] , which evaluates multiple gradient directions concurrently inside each ODE step and learns a small set of solver parameters through distillation. Unlike step-parity methods, it changes the local integration rule and requires a lightweight training stage. Recent theory also cautions against an unconstrained parallelization story: parallel-round lower bounds [ 31 ] show that some distributions necessarily retain polynomial sequential dependence. ParaLin++ is therefore formulated as a practical fixed-step parallel integrator, not as a claim that all diffusion sampling can be made depth-free. Speculative and asynchronous parallelism. A second parallel family drafts approximate future states and verifies or refines them in parallel. Diffusion speculative sampling [ 11 ] preserves the target distribution by accepting or correcting draft proposals; FREE [ 67 ] extends this idea to feature-level autoregression in DiTs; SpecDiff [ 51 ] combines self-speculation with feature caching; and DRiffusion [ 3 ] uses a draft-and-refine process. AsyncDiff [ 8 ] instead breaks component dependencies through asynchronous denoising. These methods exploit drafts, verifiers, or stale hidden states, and thus change the execution graph; ParaLin++ solves the coupled fixed-step integration system directly and does not introduce an auxiliary drafter. Step-shortening solvers and schedules. Classical high-order ODE samplers shorten the timestep grid [ 57 , 42 , 41 , 73 ] . Recent training-free variants improve this route through adaptive flow paths [ 27 ] , multirate integration for the guidance branch [ 32 ] , stiffness-aware integration [ 61 ] , and hierarchical timestep-schedule optimization [ 77 ] . These methods are relevant baselines for the quality audit, but they still alter the discretization on which prompt-conditioned trajectories depend. Per-step compute reduction and model parallelism. Orthogonal accelerators reduce the cost of each denoising evaluation. They include feature and block caching [ 49 , 48 , 40 ] , DiT attention or token sparsification [ 74 , 26 ] , temporal feature forecasting [ 36 , 18 ] , path-planned cache scheduling [ 10 ] , and distributed or asynchronous execution [ 33 , 66 , 8 ] . Guidance acceleration [ 65 ] , trajectory stitching [ 52 ] , nested diffusion [ 12 ] , and minimum-step prediction [ 72 ] are likewise complementary. These systems change the executed network path or decide when a cheaper computation is acceptable; ParaLin++ changes neither the timestep grid nor the full-step denoiser evaluation. Quality-focused evaluation. The claim that FID/CLIP evidence is insufficient is consistent with the evaluation literature: TIFA uses visual question answering to test fine-grained prompt faithfulness [ 24 ] ; VQAScore and GenAI-Bench target compositional prompts [ 34 ] ; and T2I-CompBench++ evaluates attributes, relations, and numeracy [ 25 ] . GenEval 2 additionally warns that static benchmarks can drift as generation models improve [ 28 ] . Our audit therefore interprets GenEval, DPG-Bench, and LongTextBench as a fixed, reproducible quality profile rather than as an absolute or exhaustive definition of generation quality. III Systemization of Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration We systematize training-free diffusion acceleration through the quality metrics on which its “quality-lossless” claims rest, rather than through the speed lever it uses, because FID/CLIP-style evidence does not by itself establish preservation on complex prompts. We first enumerate the evaluation protocols of the academic acceleration literature (Table I ) and identify what these methods actually measure; we then test representative few-step quality claims under a generation-quality audit and find substantial degradation (Section V , summarized in Table VI ). III-A Quality Metrics in the Training-Free Acceleration Literature Table I surveys the quality metrics used to evaluate a broad set of training-free samplers and their close relatives, from DDPM and DDIM through high-order solvers (DPM-Solver, DPMSolver++, DPM-Solver-v3, UniPC) and distillation/consistency methods, to parallel samplers (ParaDiGMS, ParaTAA, ParaSolver, ParaLin) and our ParaLin++. Two patterns are immediate. First , nearly every method is evaluated with distributional and text-alignment metrics only: FID (and its variants sFID, clean-FID) measures closeness of the generated distribution to a reference distribution, while CLIP score/CLIP-FID measures coarse prompt–image embedding similarity, and a handful additionally report Inception-based diversity (IS, Precision–Recall). These quantify statistical alignment —whether the marginal image distribution or the prompt–image embedding stays close to a reference—not whether a specific generated sample succeeds at semantic composition, dense instruction following, or long-text rendering. Second , few methods explicitly audit these generation-quality dimensions. Recent large-scale models such as FLUX [ 4 ] and Ming-Flash-Omni 2.0 [ 1 ] , in contrast, report GenEval-, DPG-Bench-, and LongTextBench-style numbers, whereas FID/CLIP are scarce or absent in their evaluation reports. A sampler certified only by FID/CLIP-style metrics can therefore appear lossless while remaining fragile on complex prompts. III-B A Realistic Quality Audit of Training-Free Accelerators The metrics gap is not cosmetic. We further test the same training-free accelerators under the generation-quality profile—GenEval, DPG-Bench, and LongTextBench—on the high-capacity FLUX.1-dev [ 4 ] , against the same-CFG 30-step Euler reference; the result is summarized in Table VI and elaborated in Section V . Methods advertised as nearly quality-lossless under FID show substantial degradation on the generation-quality metrics. Prior FID-oriented evaluations support the general expectation that reduced-step configurations can remain close to the reference distribution [ 57 , 42 , 41 , 73 ] ; in our audit, however, 16-step UniPC and DPMSolver++ cause GenEval to fall from 0.66 0.66 to 0.50 0.50 – 0.52 0.52 , DPG-Bench from 83.97 83.97 to 75.75 75.75 – 77.46 77.46 , and LongTextBench from 0.27 0.27 to 0.08 0.08 – 0.09 0.09 . An image distribution can stay FID-plausible while the model omits requested objects, breaks spatial relations, or renders unreadable text. Hence, representative training-free few-step solvers can appear nearly lossless under FID/CLIP yet lose substantially under realistic, complex quality metrics. Parallel sampling is an important exception: by preserving the full-step trajectory, it can retain near-lossless quality while removing solver latency. This failure is structural rather than incidental. Step-shortening solvers (DDIM, DPMSolver++, UniPC) buy fewer discrete steps by altering the prompt-conditioned trajectory, and the altered trajectory is what breaks dense-prompt and text fidelity; FID merely fails to reflect this break because it overlooks sample-level semantics. Parallel sampling instead keeps all N N discrete steps and removes only the solver’s temporal dependency, preserving the prompt-conditioned trajectory and the quality that depends on it. We call this the step-parity route, and ParaLin++ (Section IV-B ) is designed as its strongest realization. The rest of the paper extends the generation-quality audit (Section V ) and strengthens the step-parity solver (Sections IV – IV-B ).
